presentation_rule_original: Bitmap font and VGA colours. The gallery background surrounds the work.
presentation_rule_paper: Each pixel becomes 255 − its luminance: black becomes white, light ink becomes dark.
presentation_rule_density: Each cell becomes grey: 255 × (1 − lit pixels / 128). Colours are ignored; the real glyph bitmap determines the tone.
presentation_rule_pointillism: Seeded irregular points: area encodes intensity and colour preserves hue. Dark or light support, without a fixed white lattice.
presentation_rule_impressionism: Two layers of seeded brush marks follow the direction of local contours.
presentation_rule_graffiti: Four-level posterization, gradient contours and seeded paint speckles. An experimental stencil treatment.
presentation_gaussian_note: Gaussian approximation: separable [1, 4, 6, 4, 1] / 16 kernel at native resolution, then smooth enlargement.
presentation_export_note: Exports the whole work with its frame. Smooth enlargement depends on the browser, recorded in the recipe.
presentation_export_error: Export failed. Try a smaller scale (limit: 24 million pixels).
explore_title: One collection, several ways to look
explore_empty: No public collection is available yet.
explore_days: Selection for the work of the day
presentation_rule_reconstruction: Mix each glyph’s foreground and background by lit-pixel coverage, then interpolate cell colours. Text and fine details are softened.
presentation_rule_halftone: Regular dots of variable area encode intensity; ink hue is retained, like a colour print screen.
presentation_rule_kuwahara: Choose the mean colour of the least-variable local quadrant. Smooths surfaces while retaining major boundaries.
presentation_compare_note: Left: complete VGA rendering. Right: interpretation. The PNG exports the interpretation alone.

eda_lede: An exploration goes back and forth. You look at a figure, notice something, guess why, then test the guess with a number that could have said no. Sometimes it does, and you guess again. This page follows one such path through the museum's database.
eda_live: Every figure is computed from the live database and recomputed when the database changes. The readings were written on {date} by Claude, a language model working for the project, and nobody has reviewed them yet. Each one rests on a check that is recomputed with the figures: when a check stops holding, the page says so beside the reading.
eda_rules: Exploratory, not results: a reading becomes a result only once it is tested, as announced in advance, on packs nobody has looked at. Catalogue metadata (years, formats, SAUCE) is read over every pack. Anything measured on the grids is read from the training packs only, about four packs in five, so that the other fifth stays unseen for that test. Works the museum may not show are counted nowhere.

eda_loading: Computing the exploration from the database…
eda_unavailable: This room reads the live database: it needs the museum's local host (just museum).

eda_contents_title: 1. Before counting: what is in the database?
eda_contents_why: Every share below divides by something. So the first thing to look at is the denominators: what was acquired, what the museum can read, and what it has measured.
eda_contents_fig: From files to measurements: art works at each step of the pipeline
eda_contents_reading: The database holds {files} files from {sources} sources. {art} of them are art works, from {packs} packs. {grids} can be read as a grid ({share}). The others are formats no decoder reads yet, or files that are not what their name says (pictures and programs stamped as ANSI).
eda_contents_unread_fig: What the museum cannot read yet: art works without a grid, by format and reason
eda_contents_hyp: The pipeline's rule: a decoder is never silent. Every art work has a decoding result, either a grid or a classified error.
eda_contents_check: {missing} art works without a result at the current decoder version.
eda_contents_so: Every share below is computed over works the museum can actually read. The {unread} it cannot read are mostly RIP, RTTY and XBin files, and they are concentrated in a few years. A trend that crosses those years should be read with that gap in mind.
eda_peak_title: 2. A peak in the mid-nineties: more packs, or bigger packs?
eda_peak_why: The archive holds far more works from the mid-nineties than from any other time. But a count of works mixes two things: how many packs came out, and how many works each one held. Separating the two is the first step towards explaining the peak.
eda_peak_fig_size: Median number of art works per pack (years with at least 50 packs)
eda_peak_reading: Works peak in {works_year} ({works}). Packs peak in {packs_year} ({packs}), and the typical pack is largest in {size_year} (median {size} works). So the rise came from more packs and from bigger packs at once.
eda_peak_caution: A lesson from the way here: the first draft of this chapter found the largest packs in 1990, a year with five packs. A median over five packs says almost nothing, so the chart keeps only years with at least 50.
eda_peak_hyp: The decline after the peak is not only fewer packs: the packs shrink too.
eda_peak_check: In {year}: {late_packs} packs, against {packs} at the peak; a median of {late_size} works per pack, against {size}.
eda_peak_so: Is this the peak of the scene, or of what 16colo received? Only other archives can tell: comparing what 16colo, textfiles and Demozoo each hold gives an estimate of what all of them missed (capture–recapture, lead Q21). The packs themselves hold a clue to follow first: the SAUCE record.
eda_sauce_why: SAUCE is a 128-byte record appended to a file, with its title, author, group and date. It was proposed in 1994. Who actually wrote it is a real question: the artist's drawing program, the person who assembled the pack, or a group's habit? Each answer predicts a different pattern in the data.
eda_sauce_fig_years: Share of files with a SAUCE record, by year (years with at least 100 files)
eda_sauce_reading_years: No file has SAUCE before 1994. In {year}, {share} of ANSI files have one, and most do in the years after. ASCII files follow at a lower level and drop earlier. Both nearly vanish after 2005, then return with the editors of the 2010s.
eda_sauce_fig_packs: Packs of {year} by the share of their ANSI files that carry SAUCE (packs with at least 5 ANSI files)
eda_sauce_reading_packs: In {year}, packs are all or nothing: {none} of {packs} packs have no SAUCE at all, {all} have it on every file, and few sit in between. If each artist had decided alone, mixed packs would be common. So the decision was taken for a whole pack, or above it.
eda_sauce_hyp1: First guess: the person who assembled the pack stamped every file at once.
eda_sauce_check1: If so, every file of a fully stamped pack would carry the same date. They do not: on average such a pack holds {dates} different dates for {files} files, and only {one_date} of these packs have a single date.
eda_sauce_hyp2: Second guess: groups decided. If so, packs of the same group would make the same choice more often than chance.
eda_sauce_method: How to test it: group packs by the prefix of their name (acdu…, ice…, ciapak…, an approximation of the group). Measure how often a pack agrees with its group's majority. Then shuffle the choices between groups 2,000 times, keeping the sizes of the groups, to see what chance alone would give.
eda_sauce_fig_null: Agreement within groups: what 2,000 shuffles give, and what is observed
eda_sauce_check2: Observed {observed}; chance gives {null_mean} on average, and at most {q95} in 95% of the shuffles (p {p}; {groups} groups, {gpacks} packs).
eda_sauce_groups_fig: The largest groups of {year}: packs with SAUCE, out of their packs
eda_sauce_groups_reading: Groups disagree with one another. Packs named acdu (ACiD, the group that proposed SAUCE) carry it in {acdu}, while packs named ice (iCE, its rival) carry it in {ice}.
eda_sauce_so: A habit that spreads group by group is a diffusion process. Workstream W4 asks the same question of drawing techniques, with documented memberships and greetings instead of name prefixes, and with a null model like this one.
eda_comp_why: The shade characters ░▒▓ are a signature of ANSI art. Measured over all the ANSI files of the training packs, their share falls by about a third across the nineties. Before concluding that taste changed, check what the files are.
eda_comp_fig: Mean share of shade characters among the visible glyphs, by era
eda_comp_reading: Over all files, the share falls from {before_all} in {before} to {after_all} in {after}. Inside coloured block art it moves much less, from {before_cb} to {after_cb}. Meanwhile coloured block art went from {before_share} of the ANSI files to {after_share}: the packs filled up with text screens, which contain no shades.
eda_comp_method: Kitagawa's decomposition splits the change of a mean into two parts that add up to it: what changed inside each kind of work, and what came from the mix of kinds changing.
eda_comp_fig_split: Change of the mean shade share from {before} to {after}, in percentage points
eda_comp_hyp: Most of the fall comes from the mix of works, not from a change of hand.
eda_comp_check: Change of {total} points: {composition} from the mix of kinds, {within} within kinds.
eda_comp_so: A trend over all files can be a change in what was filed. Every comparison across years has to hold the kind of work fixed. This is Simpson's paradox in its everyday form, and the reason why the collection classifies works by what their grid holds, not by their extension.
eda_rev_title: 5. After the quiet years, did the same art come back?
eda_rev_why: After 2005 the archive almost falls silent, then fills again from 2013. A revival can repeat the old forms or change them. Two measures of the grids, on the training packs, tell which.
eda_rev_fig_rows: Median height of a work, in rows, by era
eda_rev_fig_ice: Share of works drawing more than 5% of their ink on a bright background (iCE colours), by era
eda_rev_hyp1: Works came back taller: scrolls rather than screens.
eda_rev_check1: Median height since 2013: {recent} rows, against {nineties} at most in the eras up to 2004 (a screen is 25 rows).
eda_rev_hyp2: Works came back with sixteen backgrounds instead of eight.
eda_rev_check2: iCE works since 2013: {recent}, against {nineties} at most in the eras up to 2004.
eda_rev_so: The tools changed between the two scenes: today's editors write SAUCE and offer iCE colours by default. Rule 6 of the research programme asks that the tools be ruled out before a change is credited to the artists. That is the next question to put to this data.
